source: Of all the romance books chosen from 2011–2019, only 5.5% had a non-white person on the cover.
why: The listings give 55 of 962 covers (5.7%) for 2011–2019. The 5.5% only appears for 2011–2018 (47 of 851), a period the story does not use, so the stated 2011–2019 number does not reproduce.

source: In 2022, about 14% of the full set of submissions they received for consideration — and 39% of the ones the magazine featured — had characters of color on the cover.
why: The 14% is a share of all submissions, not of the featured listings in data/listings.csv; the raw submissions dataset is not in this folder. The 39% featured share is in facts.json.

source: The rate rose to 12% in 2020, up from 7.8% when they began the survey in 2016, and has remained relatively flat since then.
why: External data from The Ripped Bodice's survey of BIPOC authors; listings.csv has no author race field.

source: In the same year, 12.3% of authors self-identified as BIPOC per The Ripped Bodice, the highest number of their survey yet.
why: External Ripped Bodice survey data; listings.csv records cover characteristics, not authors' self-identified race.

source: The Romance Writers of America, the primary association for most romance authors, estimates that 27% of romance readers identify as non-white.
why: External RWA estimate about readers; not in listings.csv.

source: Despite making up almost a quarter of the adult fiction market, the genre’s perception in the broader public imagination has often been negative
why: External market-size statistic; listings.csv covers only Publishers Weekly's featured romance titles, not the whole adult fiction market.

source: The long haired Fabio — who has graced over 400 covers — holding his tragic maiden might be the image of the romance novel that is held in the popular imagination to this day.
why: External historical count of Fabio's covers; listings.csv has no cover-model field.

source: Teal, pink, yellow, and purple make up the primary shades of romance in this style.
why: listings.csv has no cover-color field; the colors would have to be derived from the cover images, which are not provided.

source: Books in the historical, gothic, and fantasy subgenres hold out as rare stalwarts of their original style.
This was known as “the clinch”, which had its peak in the 1970s and 1980s.
why: Historical claim about decades before the 2011–2023 listings; the dataset cannot show the 1970s–1980s peak.

source: In the 50s and 60s, when many more women joined the workforce, corporate romance and doctor-nurse covers were popular.
why: Historical claim about the 1950s–1960s; the dataset begins in 2011.

source: In the 70s and 80s, clinch covers represented an era of more feminist openness in women’s sexual desire, challenging puritan social forces, and juxtaposing the two in the social eye.
why: Historical interpretation of 1970s–1980s covers; the dataset begins in 2011 and has no measure of feminist openness.

source: with the rise of commercial plane travel, women appeared in scenes abroad, often with highly exoticized supporting characters.
why: Historical claim about mid-20th-century covers; not measurable in the 2011–2023 listings.
